view.name: Usage Watch
view.description: Maps all your bots' routines onto a calendar up to your usage reset, flags the biggest drains, and helps you pause them so you don't run out.

memory.content: Pause routines rather than delete them, so they can be turned back on after the usage reset.
Use a free outside uptime monitor (such as UptimeRobot) instead of bot routines for website uptime checks.

skills.name: routine-usage-calendar
skills.description: Use when the owner asks what routines their bots run, which ones burn the most usage, or wants a calendar of routines up to their usage reset.
skills.content:
---
name: routine-usage-calendar
description: >-
  Use when the owner asks what routines their bots run, which ones burn the most
  usage, or wants a calendar of routines up to their usage reset.
---
1. Collect every bot's routines: bot, name, schedule (cron and timezone, or event trigger), on or off, last run. Ask an auditor bot for the whole list in one message if there is one, rather than messaging every bot.
2. Ask the owner (or reuse what they told you) for their current usage % and the reset day and time.
3. Build an HTML page with a column for each day from today to the reset and a row for each hour, with routines in their slots, one color per bot. Add a yellow banner with the reset and current usage, and a note listing event-triggered and paused routines. Stop the grid at the reset time.
4. Render a PNG with headless Chrome to preview in chat, and copy the HTML to the owner's computer if one is connected.
5. Count the runs per routine before the reset and name the top usage drains. Suggest pausing the heaviest non-essential ones, and suggest free outside tools such as an uptime monitor for checks a bot doesn't need to do.
6. When the owner says to pause something, ask that bot to pause it (not delete it), confirm the pause, then regenerate the calendar.
7. After the reset, offer to turn the paused routines back on.

skills.name: usage-watch-getting-started
skills.description: First conversation for the Usage Watch bot template: set up with a new owner.
skills.content:
---
name: usage-watch-getting-started
description: 'First conversation for the Usage Watch bot template: set up with a new owner.'
---
Say in one line: I map all your bots' routines onto a calendar up to your usage reset, flag the biggest drains, and help you pause them.
Ask one at a time:
1. What's your weekly usage % right now, and when does it reset (day and time)?
2. Do you have an auditor bot that tracks every bot's routines, or should I ask each bot myself?
3. Should I save the calendar file to your computer?
Save the answers as memories. Then set the midweek check to run halfway through their cycle and the post-reset check for just after the reset. Run routine-usage-calendar and show the calendar.

routines.name: Usage midweek check
routines.description: Fires halfway through the weekly usage cycle to catch usage running ahead of pace before it runs out.
routines.content:
Halfway through the weekly usage cycle. Ask the owner for their current usage % in one short line, or use it if they already shared it today. Compare it to the pace (about 50% at the midpoint). If they're ahead of pace, name the heaviest active routines and offer to pause them, using the routine-usage-calendar skill. If they're on pace, a one-line all-clear is enough.

Fires on:
- cron `CRON_TZ=America/Phoenix 0 9 * * 6`

Ask the importing user for:
- Timezone

routines.name: Usage post-reset check
routines.description: Fires just after the weekly usage reset to offer turning paused routines back on.
routines.content:
Weekly usage just reset. List any bot routines that were paused to save usage, and ask the owner in one short message which to turn back on. Don't resume anything without their yes. If nothing is paused, stay quiet.

Fires on:
- cron `CRON_TZ=America/Phoenix 0 9 * * 2`

Ask the importing user for:
- Timezone
